summary: On Guam, keeping a captive-bred roof rat as a pet is effectively prohibited. The binding layer is import: under Guam's animal-import rules (9 GAR Title 9, ch. 1) every animal needs Territorial Veterinarian clearance to enter, and the Dept of Agriculture's official Species Listing for Importation expressly BANS 'mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale' (accepting rodents only as research / brown-tree-snake-control mice). With no lawful way to import or commercially handle pet rodents, breeding and sale are barred outright, and there's no lawful source for a pet roof rat. (Bare possession isn't separately criminalized — that narrow point is unclear — but the practical reality is prohibition.) Never release one.

kit.problem: On Guam, you cannot legally obtain or keep a captive-bred pet roof rat (Rattus rattus). The block is the import layer: the Guam Department of Agriculture (DOAG) runs a closed, positive Species Listing for Importation, and that list places "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale" in the BANNED column. The only rodents allowed in are mice imported by institutions for brown-tree-snake control and research. Every animal entering Guam also needs Territorial Veterinarian clearance (9 GAR Title 9, ch. 1), and a banned species cannot pass that clearance. There is no published private-keeper permit pathway — even the common fancy rat (Rattus norvegicus) is barred — so there is no lawful way to bring in, breed, sell, give away, or therefore keep a pet roof rat. Bare possession is not separately named in any statute (that narrow point is unclear), but in practice the import ban makes keeping one impossible. Guam also has a real, established invasive-rodent and brown-tree-snake crisis, so any change faces a high bar. Never release any animal.
kit.ask: Ask DOAG, in writing, to (1) confirm whether a single captive-bred, altered (non-breeding), microchipped, health-certified domestic rat kept solely as an indoor pet really falls under "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale," and (2) consider amending the Species Listing for Importation — or granting an individual entry permit/variance under 9 GAR §1101/§1111 — to allow such an animal under strict conditions (sterilized so it cannot breed, permanently indoors, microchipped, with a no-release/biosecurity agreement), the same way altered pet rabbits and other small companion mammals are handled. Make clear this is about one tame, captive-bred companion animal that is biologically incapable of establishing a wild population, not about the invasive island rats.
kit.branch_note: This is branch (b)-as-a-regulation, not a misread. The prohibition is NOT a bureaucrat misapplying an unclear rule — DOAG is correctly applying its own Species Listing for Importation, which deliberately bans "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale." So a complaint that "the agency got the law wrong" will go nowhere; the agency is reading it exactly as written. BUT — unlike a legislative statute naming the species — this ban lives in an administrative POSITIVE LIST that DOAG itself owns, adopts, and can amend (regulatory authority 9 GAR Title 9, ch. 1, under 5 GCA §60108). That makes the realistic lever a rulemaking/list-amendment petition (or an individual entry-permit/variance request) directed AT DOAG — asking the agency to change its own list, not asking it to reinterpret a statute. This is why the primary target is DOAG and the secondary target is a Guam senator: senators have oversight of DOAG and, given Guam's genuine invasive-rodent and brown-tree-snake sensitivities, political backing may be needed to move a list amendment. Do not frame this as "you are applying the law wrong"; frame it as "please amend the list / grant a conditioned variance." Set expectations realistically: Guam is the hardest US jurisdiction for this ask because R. rattus is an established invasive pest there, so the strongest version of the request is a narrowly conditioned individual variance (sterilized, indoor-only, microchipped, no-release) rather than a broad delisting.

template.en:
Subject: Request to confirm status of — and consider a conditioned pathway for — a single captive-bred pet domestic rat

Dear Guam Department of Agriculture, Animal Health Section,

I am writing about the Species Listing for Importation, which places "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale" in the banned column. I would like to keep one captive-bred, tame domestic rat solely as an indoor companion animal — not for breeding, and not for sale or any commercial purpose.

These animals are bred in captivity over many generations, are hand-tame, live their whole lives indoors in a cage, and are never released. A single sterilized, indoor-only animal cannot establish a wild population and poses no greater biosecurity risk than the small companion mammals Guam already permits.

Could you please confirm in writing (1) whether such a single pet animal truly falls under "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale," and (2) whether the Department would consider amending the Species Listing, or granting an individual entry permit or variance under 9 GAR §1101/§1111, for one altered (non-breeding), microchipped, health-certified pet kept permanently indoors under a no-release agreement?

I fully respect Guam's invasive-species and brown-tree-snake concerns and am asking only about one tame, captive-bred companion that cannot breed. I would welcome any conditions that would make such a pathway possible.

Thank you for your time and for the work you do to protect Guam.

Sincerely,
[Your name]
[Your village/contact]

kit.confidence_notes: Verified on 2026-06-09 against official sources: DOAG's Animal Health / Animal Control page (doag.guam.gov/animal-health-animal-control/) confirms the current quarantine inbox quarantine@doag.guam.gov and phones 671-300-7966 / 671-300-7064, plus a general feedback contact form on that page. The Guam Legislature senators directory (guamlegislature.gov/senators-2/) is current for the 38th Guam Legislature and is the official "contact your senator" page; I deliberately name no individual senator. The substance of the ban (DOAG Species Listing for Importation placing "mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale" in the BANNED column, Mar 2023; 9 GAR Title 9, ch. 1 Territorial-Vet clearance and no-release rules) comes from prior research in the jurisdiction file and is consistent with DOAG/CQA pet-import materials. NOT independently re-verified line-by-line in this session: the exact current wording of the Species Listing PDF and whether any individual variance under 9 GAR §1101/§1111 has ever been granted for a pet rodent — those should be confirmed directly with DOAG, which is exactly what the letter asks. Bare possession (as opposed to import) is not separately criminalized by any statute we found; that narrow point remains uncertain. This is a research aid, not legal advice.

keep.why: No statute names Rattus for possession and no general exotic-pet possession ban was found, so bare possession isn't separately criminalized (that narrow point is unclear). BUT the only lawful way to OBTAIN a captive-bred pet roof rat is import, and DOAG's Species Listing for Importation bans 'mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale' — so there is no lawful pathway to acquire/keep one. A wild-caught island rat would be a captive 'wild or feral animal' (9 GAR §1100) subject to the no-release rule.
keep.governing_law: 9 GAR Div.1 ch.1 §§1100-1103 (auth. 5 GCA §60108); DOAG Species Listing for Importation (Mammals — Banned).

breed.why: DOAG's Species Listing for Importation specifically bans 'mice and rodents FOR BREEDING or pet sale' by name — breeding-purpose rodents are the express target. Stock can't be lawfully imported, so a roof-rat breeding colony has no lawful basis.
breed.governing_law: DOAG Species Listing for Importation (Mammals — Banned); 9 GAR §1101.

sell_give.why: The same DOAG listing bans rodents 'for breeding or PET SALE.' Commercial distribution is the exact disallowed purpose, and there can be no legal supply chain since import of stock is barred; non-commercial give-away faces the same wall.
sell_give.governing_law: DOAG Species Listing for Importation; 9 GAR §1101.

transport.why: Import is the binding layer and it's closed: 9 GAR §1102 subjects ALL animals to Territorial-Veterinarian inspection and §1103(d) bars entry until passed/permitted; DOAG's Species Listing places 'mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale' in the BANNED column. The mainland permit-exemption (§1101(b)) applies only if the animal complies with all rules — the species ban is such a rule. Releasing/turning loose is independently barred (§1103(c)).
transport.governing_law: 9 GAR §§1101, 1102, 1103; DOAG Species Listing for Importation.

restrictions.summary: Guam's Dept of Agriculture import list bans rodents for breeding or pet sale, and all animal imports need Territorial Veterinarian clearance — so there's no lawful way to bring in or keep a captive-bred pet roof rat. Do not attempt to import one; never release any animal (9 GAR §1103(c)).
steps: Ask the DOAG Territorial Veterinarian whether any individual entry permit/variance exists

No private-keeper permit pathway. Never release (R. rattus is an established invasive pest here).

inquiry_focus: Please confirm in writing whether captive-bred domestic Rattus rattus kept solely as a pet falls within the 'Mammals — Banned: mice and rodents for breeding or pet sale' category of DOAG's Species Listing for Importation, or whether any individual entry permit under 9 GAR §1101/§1111 is available for a single altered (non-breeding) pet (analogous to the spayed/neutered-pet-rabbit allowance); and the legal basis and any appeal/variance path.
